title: Prison (Genesis 39–40)
hook: a false accusation, prison, and a forgotten favor

segments.voice: Yesterday, bor: a dry cistern, a coat dipped in goat's blood, and a brother sold to traders bound for Egypt. Your line was sold by his own.

Egypt. Joseph is a slave now, still a young man, bought by an officer of Pharaoh named Potiphar. And something odd happens: everything he touches goes well. Soon he's running the whole house. Then his master's wife starts noticing him, day after day, and one day, when no one else is inside, she grabs him by his cloak. He runs, and leaves the cloak in her hand. She holds up the cloak and says he attacked her: the second time Joseph's clothes have been turned into a lie, after the coat in goat's blood. Potiphar believes her. Joseph goes to prison.
screen: `A SLAVE IN POTIPHAR'S HOUSE.` → `A CLOAK LEFT IN HER HAND.` → `PRISON.`

segments.voice: Read chapter thirty-nine slowly and one phrase keeps coming back: the Lord was with Joseph. It's there when he's a slave in Potiphar's house, when his master sees everything prospering in his hands, and twice in the prison. "But the Lord was with Joseph," the Douay-Rheims reads, and soon the keeper of the prison puts him in charge of the other prisoners. Not on the day he's made governor: in the slave quarters and the cell. The text never says God got him out. It says God was with him in it. Second, what Joseph does when no one is looking. He refused his master's wife with two reasons: it would betray the man who trusted him with everything, and it would be a sin against God. Nobody was watching. That was the whole test. Third, the forgotten favor. Two of Pharaoh's officials land in the same prison: the chief butler, who poured Pharaoh's wine, and the chief baker. Each has a dream. One morning Joseph sees their sad faces and asks why. Interpretations belong to God, he says, then tells them: in three days the butler goes back to his post, and the baker dies. Both come true. Joseph asks the butler one thing: remember me to Pharaoh. And the chapter ends flatly. The butler forgot him. Two full years go by. Centuries later, a psalm remembers this stretch: his feet humbled in fetters, iron around him, until God's word came. The chapter doesn't hurry past the waiting, and it never calls it wasted.
screen: `THE LORD WAS WITH JOSEPH, IN THE CELL.` · `HE SAID NO WHEN NO ONE WAS WATCHING.` · `REMEMBER ME. THE BUTLER FORGOT.` · `A PSALM REMEMBERS THE FETTERS.`

segments.voice: Find one moment in your day that nobody's checking, the dishes in the sink, a receipt slightly wrong in your favor, what you say about someone who isn't there, and picture doing the right thing in it, quietly, with no audience. If you pray, carry the chapter's phrase, the Lord was with Joseph; if you don't, just hold the choice and let it settle.
Prison. In Genesis, the place Joseph lands on a false charge, and where the text says, twice, the Lord was with him. Today's word.
Your line: the lord was with joseph. Not after the cell, but in it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Joseph story is read at Mass on a weekday in Lent, and Psalm 105 (104 in the Douay numbering), which remembers Joseph in fetters, is among the psalms of the Liturgy of the Hours.

original.note: Hebrew: the prison in Joseph's story. the word sohar is rare outside these chapters, and its exact sense is uncertain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bad chapter before the good part.
what it means: a slave, then a prisoner on a false charge, and the text keeps saying the Lord was with him there.
what a scholar hears: the phrase frames Genesis 39 from the house to the cell, and the prison gets a rare Hebrew name, beit ha-sohar.

chat.says: If God was with Joseph, why was he stuck in prison for years?
options: The text says God was with him in the cell, not that God got him out.
God was only with him once he got out and became governor.
Joseph forgot God in prison, so God waited for him to come back.
chat.meaning: Genesis says the Lord was with Joseph in the slave quarters and twice in the prison. It never says God got him out; God was with him in it.

Potiphar.meaning: the officer of Pharaoh who bought Joseph

chief butler.meaning: the official who poured Pharaoh's wine

sources.quoted: But the Lord was with Joseph

notes: 'The Lord was with Joseph/him' appears in some form at Genesis 39:2, 39:3, 39:21 and 39:23; the script says 'twice in the prison' (39:21, 39:23). Confirm against the Douay-Rheims wording.
Joseph's two reasons for refusing (betraying his master's trust; sin against God) paraphrase Genesis 39:8–9.
Beit ha-sohar (Genesis 39:20–23; 40:3, 5): the sense of sohar ('round house'?) is debated; confirm the note.

Joseph as a type of Christ is a standard patristic and Catholic reading; howItsDone says the Joseph story is read at weekday Mass in Lent (Genesis 37 on the Friday of the second week of Lent in the current lectionary).
